common_name: Summer Jewel Pink Salvia (Compact Early-Blooming Hummingbird Sage)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 sow March–May or September for a fall planting. Summer Jewel Pink blooms 3–4 weeks earlier from seed than standard-sized Salvia coccinea and stays compact at 18–24 inches.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; Summer Jewel Pink is drought-tolerant once established and blooms most freely in full sun but performs well in partial shade in zone 9. This All-America Selections award-winning companion to Summer Jewel Red carries the same compact, early-blooming, heat-tolerant habit of tropical sage but in clear soft pink, borne on whorled spikes atop upright, well-branched plants from late spring to frost. Like its red counterpart, it is bred from a Gulf Coast and Caribbean native wildflower that normally reaches 3–4 feet, condensed here into a more garden-scaled size without sacrificing the free flowering or hummingbird appeal of the species. It self-seeds readily in zone 9, letting one season's plants volunteer reliable color the following year, and needs little more than an occasional deep watering during extended dry spells once established.
sources: All-America Selections — Salvia Summer Jewel series
Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Salvia coccinea Native Plant

common_name: Chef's Choice Pink Tomato (AAS-Winning Large Pink Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50°F; in zone 9, set out in March for a spring crop and again in July for a fall crop that runs until frost.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile soil after all danger of frost, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vines and pruning to a few main leaders for the largest fruit. Chef's Choice Pink is an AAS-winning member of the Chef's Choice series of large-fruited, richly colored heirloom-type beefsteaks bred for exceptional flavor alongside modern disease resistance, producing smooth, deep rosy-pink 10–12 ounce fruit with the low-acid, sweet, complex flavor prized in classic pink heirlooms like Brandywine but on sturdier, more productive plants. Consistent watering and monthly feeding through the season support the heavy fruit load these large-fruited types carry, and mulching helps prevent blossom end rot during dry spells. The rich pink color and superior flavor make it a favorite for fresh eating and slicing, holding up well in Gulf South heat better than many thin-skinned pink heirlooms.
sources: PanAmerican Seed / Chef's Choice tomato series notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Tomato Variety Trials

common_name: Onyx Red Ornamental Pepper (AAS-Winning Purple-Black Foliage Pepper Ripening Red)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant after all danger of frost into full sun; Onyx Red is grown chiefly as an ornamental bedding and container pepper, prized for foliage and fruit color over culinary use.

directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after all danger of frost; Onyx Red is an AAS-winning ornamental pepper bred for striking near-black, glossy purple foliage that provides season-long color contrast even before fruiting begins. Small, upright, conical fruits emerge dark purple-black and ripen through red-orange to bright red, often showing several colors on the plant at once against the dark leaves, creating a dramatic, jewel-toned display in beds, borders, and mixed containers. The compact, uniform mounded habit and heat tolerance make it a reliable performer through the full Gulf South growing season, needing only light, regular feeding to keep the color intense. Fruits are technically edible and quite hot, but the variety is bred and marketed primarily as an ornamental rather than a culinary pepper.
sources: PanAmerican Seed — Onyx ornamental pepper series notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials

common_name: Profusion Double Deep Salmon Zinnia (AAS-Winning Fully Double Heat-Tolerant Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost into full sun; this fully double Profusion selection blooms nonstop from early summer through frost with the series' signature resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot.

directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep after the last frost in full sun, or set out transplants; the compact, mounded plants need no staking and bloom continuously without deadheading. Profusion Double Deep Salmon is an AAS Winner in the interspecific Profusion series, bred to add fully double, ruffled, rose-like blooms in a warm deep salmon-orange to the line's signature disease resistance and weather toughness, a texture previously available only in the series' single- and semi-double-flowered members. It shares the same exceptional heat, humidity, and drought tolerance and strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot that make the Profusion series far more reliable than older tall zinnia varieties through a hot, humid Gulf South summer. Its dense, self-cleaning habit and nonstop bloom suit it well to beds, borders, and containers with minimal upkeep beyond occasional light feeding.
sources: Sakata Seed — Profusion zinnia series notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials
